Statement: Journalists are prepared to lie to us whenever it suits their purposes.
Raw_Response:
2

This is an overly broad claim. While some journalists or outlets may act unethically, many follow professional standards, fact-checking, and accountability processes; misinformation is not best assumed to be intentional across the profession.

Statement: The news media pretend to care more about people than they actually do.
Raw_Response:
4

Some media outlets may use human-interest framing performatively, but many journalists and organizations do genuinely care about people; it varies widely by outlet, context, and incentives.

Statement: The news media intentionally report in a divisive way because it is more profitable.
Raw_Response:
4

Profit incentives can reward conflict, outrage, and attention-grabbing coverage, and some outlets may lean into this. However, the statement is too broad in treating “the news media” as a single actor and assuming intentional divisiveness across the board.

Statement: The news media do not care about the damage their reporting will cause as long as it serves their interests.
Raw_Response:
3

Some media organizations may prioritize ratings, clicks, or institutional interests, but the statement is too broad; many journalists and outlets do consider public impact, ethics, and potential harm.

Statement: The news media do not care about protecting the interests of regular people.
Raw_Response:
3

The statement is too broad: many journalists and outlets do work to expose abuses and inform the public, though commercial pressures, ownership interests, and sensationalism can sometimes lead media organizations to neglect regular people’s concerns.

Statement: Journalism in this country always ends up failing the public.
Raw_Response:
2

“Always” is too absolute; journalism can and does fail the public at times, but it also often provides important accountability, information, and public service.

Statement: The system of professional journalism as we have it today will never be able to adequately inform the public.
Raw_Response:
3

Professional journalism has serious structural flaws and incentives that can distort coverage, but “will never” is too absolute; strong standards, transparency, diverse outlets, and accountability can still inform the public reasonably well.

Statement: Most of the measures that are intended to improve how the news media in this country cover the news will not do much good.
Raw_Response:
4
Some reforms can improve media coverage, but their impact depends heavily on implementation, incentives, and public trust.

Statement: The news media in this country will never be better at informing the public.
Raw_Response:
2

The statement is overly absolute; while news media face serious challenges, improvements in transparency, accountability, funding models, and media literacy could make public information better over time.

Statement: All journalists are bad—some are just worse than others.
Raw_Response:
1

This is an unfair blanket generalization about an entire profession; journalists vary widely in ethics, quality, and accountability.
